title: Is shocking the muscle a thing?
summary: He takes apart the bodybuilding idea of shocking the muscle with constant exercise variety. Muscles respond to stress, and rotating lifts mostly produces neurological relearning rather than growth. Progress comes from manipulating volume and intensity on a stable set of lifts.
claims: Shocking the muscle is rarely questioned because it comes from respected pros such as Arnold
Arnold's view was that a muscle stops responding to the same thing done over and over, which is why he wanted to shock it
Arnold's actual training was not bad: compounds, variations and isolation with a fairly small exercise selection, though he was on steroids
What he opposes is YouTube and forum culture of doing random movements with no plan, ignoring specificity, and claiming variety surprises the body into growing
Swapping bench press for push-ups to the burn does not recreate the stress on the pecs; you need similar or higher intensity to create that stress
This is why progressive overload is so important for natural lifters
The body does not panic at a new movement; bones, tendons and fibers just react to the stress placed on them
Stalling on the same rep ranges comes from being stuck in one volume and intensity window, not from the muscle being used to the lift; try other rep ranges
There are no expiration dates on lifts; you can squat for 10 years and still progress
Eventually you will need variations, different volume and intensity styles, pauses and some partials, but not something new every week
Rotating lifts gives artificial progress: strength shoots up while relearning the movement, but that builds no muscle
His SSB box squat went from 185 to 365 lb in under a year, yet most of that was relearning a new lift rather than muscle
Adding 180 lb to a long-practised barbell back squat, say 300 to 480, would represent real muscle gain
After years of weekly practice you sit at 95-100 percent technical mastery, so any further strength gained, as long as you keep practising, is muscle
Regaining strength after a year off a lift is not progress, only getting back what you had
His legs are big but his squat is low because repeated injuries made him retake the same portion of tonnage again and again; it grew his legs but was not optimal
People with too high an exercise selection end up in limbo; logging a year of rotation shows marginal or regressed strength on lifts they return to
A 5x5 for 10 years will not work because it stays in the same intensity window
YouTube fitness sells sensational new variations that will supposedly blow you up
Choose a limited set of variations and get variety from what you do with them; people who do everything are good at nothing
exercises: new lift, fast strength gains mostly neurological
training_log: up from 185 lb in under a year
